Heatwave Condenser Lab

Heatwave Condenser Lab

Design the equipment, then test it. Step 1 sizes a fin-and-tube coil, a shell-and-tube condenser and a cooling tower from your room temperature, the outdoor design temperature and the dimensions you choose. Step 2 runs both chillers through a whole heatwave day and shows which keeps the hospital room cool, and at what cost in electricity and water.

What the words mean

ChillerA machine that takes heat out of a room's water loop and throws it outside, using a refrigerant, a compressor and two heat exchangers.
CondenserThe heat exchanger where the refrigerant gives its heat away to the outside and turns back into liquid. This project compares two kinds.
Condensing temperatureHow hot the refrigerant is while it gives heat away. It must be hotter than the outside sink, so a hotter day forces it higher.
Dry-bulb vs wet-bulbDry-bulb is the normal air temperature. Wet-bulb is what a wet cloth in the wind reaches: evaporation cools it, more so in dry air.
Capacity and shortfallCapacity is the most cooling the chiller can give right now. If the room needs more, the gap is the shortfall and the room warms.
Design dayThe hot-but-normal day each chiller is sized for, with 10 % spare capacity. A heatwave goes beyond it.
Wet padA wetted mat the air passes through before the coil. Water evaporates and cools the air, at the cost of water.
COP and kWhCOP is cooling delivered per unit of electricity. kWh is energy: 1 kW running for 1 hour.
Fin pitch and fin efficiencyFin pitch is the spacing between fins. Fin efficiency says how well the far parts of a fin still help: 100 % would mean the whole fin is at tube temperature.
Approach and rangeRange: how much the tower cools the water. Approach: how close the cold water gets to the wet-bulb. A small approach needs a taller tower.
U and UAU is heat flow per m² per °C of temperature difference; UA multiplies by the area. A bigger UA moves more heat for the same temperature gap.
Merkel numberKaV/L measures how much evaporative cooling the tower fill must provide. Higher means a taller tower.

The model in plain words

1 · Room load

The fresh-air term uses enthalpy, so humid air adds latent (moisture) load: the mass-transfer part. A colder room setting means more load and a colder evaporator.

2 · Fin-and-tube coil

Air side ho from the Wang (2000) plain-fin correlation, refrigerant side hi from Shah (1979), fin efficiency from the equal-area circle we verified with ANSYS. Rows = UA needed ÷ UA per row.

3 · Shell-and-tube condenser

Shell side: Nusselt film condensation on tubes with Kern's row correction. Tube side: Gnielinski. Tube count from water flow and velocity, length from area, shell diameter from the Sinnott bundle formula.

4 · Cooling tower

Merkel's method: water is cooled by evaporation driven by the enthalpy difference between saturated air at the water temperature and the passing air. Fill height = required KaV/L ÷ fill rating per metre.

5 · Compressor

From R134a property tables. A higher condensing temperature means more work per kg and less refrigerant pumped, so capacity falls on hot days.

6 · The day simulation

Every 30 simulated seconds the condensing temperature is solved where the built condenser (and tower) can reject exactly what the compressor delivers. If cooling falls short, the room warms.

This is a simplified, physics-based model built for a course project. Weather days use reported peak temperatures; room loads, humidity and several equipment values are our assumptions. It shows trends and trade-offs, not exact numbers for a real building.
